module: Celiac Disease and Small Bowel Enteropathies

steps.say: Cow milk allergy wears two very different masks, and mixing them up delays the right plan. One child breaks into hives within minutes of a sip, while another vomits violently hours later with no rash at all. The four panel hypersensitivity chart here maps that split beautifully, with immediate IgE reactions on one side and delayed cell driven injury on the other. Learn which child fits which panel before ordering a single test.
steps.tx: Separate the **IgE vs non-IgE phenotypes** at the first visit. Cow milk protein allergy encompasses IgE-mediated reactions (hives, wheeze or anaphylaxis starting within 2 hours of ingestion) and non-IgE-mediated gastrointestinal syndromes (food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome, allergic proctocolitis and enteropathy, all delayed by hours). A history of rapid hives points to IgE testing and adrenaline planning, while delayed vomiting or bloody stools without hives points to elimination and supervised challenge instead.

vis.alt: Diagram of Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity types 1 to 4 with mechanisms and clinical examples.
vis.caption: Four mechanisms cover allergy, cytotoxic injury, complex deposition, and delayed T cell reactions. Each mechanism indicates its own workup. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: A happy thriving breastfed baby with streaks of blood in the nappy terrifies parents, yet the outlook is reassuring. This pattern typically appears between two and eight weeks of life, with mucus streaked stools but steady weight gain and smiles. The culprit is usually maternal dairy passing through breast milk. Reassure the family, keep breastfeeding going, and adjust the maternal diet rather than reaching for formula.
steps.tx: Recognise **food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis** in breastfed infants aged 2-8 weeks with visible blood and mucus streaks in stool despite normal growth and a happy, thriving demeanor. The infant feeds well, vomits little and gains weight, which separates this benign entity from enterocolitis or surgical causes. Maternal dairy exclusion usually clears the bleeding within days, and the condition resolves entirely by late infancy without lasting gut injury.

steps.say: Contrast that settled baby with the infant who vomits again and again after a feed and then goes limp and pale. Repetitive forceful emesis starting one to four hours after milk, followed by cold hands, sleepiness and sometimes shock, defines enterocolitis syndrome. These children dehydrate fast and need urgent fluids. The dehydration grading chart here, with its ORS plans, guides exactly how aggressively to rehydrate each case.
steps.tx: Spot **FPIES presentation and shock** early. Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES, a delayed gut allergy) causes profuse repetitive emesis 1-4 hours post-ingestion leading to dehydration, hypothermia (low body temperature), methemoglobinemia (altered haemoglobin reducing oxygen carriage), and hypovolemic shock (circulatory collapse from fluid loss). Admit pale, lethargic or hypotensive infants for intravenous fluids and monitoring, and teach parents that future exposures need an emergency action plan with hospital access.

vis.alt: Reference chart with dehydration grading table by four clinical signs, ORS composition and Plans A, B and C illustrations.
vis.caption: Dehydration grading with ORS Plans A, B and C. Neonatal maintenance fluids reach 100 to 130 mL per kg per day by day 4. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Choosing the right substitute milk matters as much as making the diagnosis. For mild to moderate disease in a formula fed baby, an extensively hydrolysed feed, where milk proteins are chopped tiny, settles most cases. Reserve the fully elemental amino acid feed for severe disease, faltering growth or anaphylaxis. Never advise a partially hydrolysed or ordinary lactose free formula, since both still carry enough protein to trigger symptoms.
steps.tx: Prescribe **extensively hydrolyzed formula first-line** for mild-to-moderate CMPA in formula-fed infants. Extensively hydrolyzed formula (eHF, milk protein broken into tiny peptides) resolves symptoms in the large majority, while amino acid formula (AAF, elemental building blocks only) is reserved for severe disease, growth failure or anaphylaxis. Reassess at every visit, because continuing an unneeded elemental formula wastes money and burdens families, and failed eHF trials should prompt escalation rather than persistence.

steps.say: When the baby is exclusively breastfed, the treatment runs through the mother, not the infant. She must cut out every source of dairy, reading labels for whey and casein, while protecting her own bones with calcium. One thousand milligrams of calcium daily, through diet or supplements, keeps her skeleton safe during months of exclusion. Support her closely, because unnecessary prolonged restriction harms maternal nutrition and morale alike.
steps.tx: Maintain the **maternal elimination diet** in exclusively breastfed infants with suspected CMPA. The mother follows strict exclusion of all dairy products with calcium supplementation of 1000 mg/day (through tablets or fortified foods), plus vitamin D, while breastfeeding continues uninterrupted. Review her diet for hidden dairy in bakery and processed foods, monitor infant stools and growth, and plan a supervised maternal reintroduction once the infant passes structured challenge testing.

rows: All milk, cheese, yoghurt, whey, casein

steps.say: Soy formula tempts families as a cheap fix, but it is the wrong answer for young infants. Below six months the gut cross reacts to soy in up to one in seven babies, and the feed itself carries phytates and plant oestrogens you do not want early on. Reserve soy for older infants only after specialist review. For the young baby with proven allergy, hydrolysed or elemental feeds remain the safe choice.
steps.tx: Observe the **soy formula age limitation** strictly. Soy infant formula is not recommended under 6 months of age due to phytate content (mineral binding compounds), isoflavone phytoestrogens (plant hormones), and concomitant cross-reactivity in up to 10-15% of milk allergic infants. Even beyond six months, introduce soy only with documented tolerance and growth monitoring. Counsel families against unsupervised soy switching, which masks ongoing gut inflammation while appearing cheaper.

steps.say: Here is the good news every parent needs to hear: most children outgrow this allergy. More than half tolerate milk by their first birthday, and eight to nine out of ten are free by school entry. Prove it safely with a supervised food challenge in hospital every six to twelve months, stepping up doses under observation. Never test at home, because a severe reactor can still surprise you even after a long quiet spell.
steps.tx: Track **natural tolerance development** with scheduled reassessment. Tolerance develops in over 50% of CMPA children by 1 year of age and exceeds 80-90% by 3-5 years, reassessed via supervised oral food challenge at 6-12 month intervals in a hospital setting with resuscitation available. Between challenges, maintain the elimination strictly, because accidental exposures reset confidence but do not usually accelerate tolerance. Document each challenge outcome carefully to guide nursery and school planning.

nodes.label: Tolerance by 1 year in over half

steps.say: For children who react to fresh milk yet sail through muffins, the baked milk ladder offers a delicious shortcut. Heating unravels the trigger shapes in milk protein, so many allergic children tolerate cakes and biscuits long before a glass of milk. Climbing the ladder from crumbs to custard under guidance builds tolerance faster and delights the child. Keep adrenaline handy during steps, and retreat one rung after any reaction.
steps.tx: Use the **baked milk ladder** for children who tolerate baked milk (muffins and cookies where heat denatures conformational epitopes, the folded trigger shapes). Such children develop resolution of unheated milk allergy significantly faster when advanced stepwise from baked crumbs through pancakes to fresh milk under medical supervision. Each rung needs a symptom diary and a clear retreat rule, and any systemic reaction pauses climbing until specialist review resets the pace.
